question: Use a ridge plot to compare the distribution of tumor mutational burden (TMB) across 10 cancer types.

files.eval_guideline: Ridge plot must show TMB density distributions for all 10 cancer types as stacked overlapping curves; axis labels, color scheme, and cancer type ordering may differ.
files.match_reasoning: Both paths have the identical filename tmb_ridge_plot.png and indicate PNG images. The filename and shared task identifier directly correspond to the requested ridge plot comparing TMB distributions across 10 cancer types.
files.strategy_reasoning: The guideline requires a ridge plot showing TMB density distributions for all 10 cancer types as stacked overlapping curves, while allowing labels, colors, and ordering to vary. Semantic comparison evaluates these visual requirements without requiring pixel-level agreement.

comparison_details.explanation: Both images show stacked, filled TMB density ridges for the same 10 cancer types in the same order: Melanoma, Lung Adenocarcinoma, Bladder, Colorectal, Head & Neck, Stomach, Breast, Pancreatic, Ovarian, and Prostate. The distribution shapes, relative locations, spreads, and right-skewed tails closely match. Both convey the same scientific message: melanoma has the highest and broadest TMB distribution, followed by lung adenocarcinoma and bladder, while ovarian and prostate cancers have the lowest and most concentrated distributions. Both horizontal axes express mutations per megabase. The candidate adds dashed median markers, numerical medians, sample sizes, and an explicit Gaussian KDE description; these annotations are absent from the reference and cannot be independently verified from it, but are visually consistent with the distributions. Differences in colors, label placement, gridlines, and horizontal extent (approximately 33 versus 37) do not materially affect interpretation because the visible density lies within both ranges. Both satisfy the requirement for 10 stacked ridge distributions with overlap visible among the lower curves. No cancer type or critical scientific element is missing.
